question: In a Philadelphia suburb, which incoming children fully mastered the city's intricate rule for the short a vowel?
options: Those who arrived before age eight
All who had lived there six years
answer: Mainly those with Philadelphia-born parents. In Arvilla Payne's study, children of out-of-state parents picked up the simpler local vowels, especially if they arrived young, but rarely the short a rule, which works word by word: mad and bad take one vowel, sad another. It had to be heard at home.
move: What has to be learned case by case passes through close contact.
trap: Trusting early arrival alone to give a child the full local accent.
reference: Payne, Factors controlling the acquisition of the Philadelphia dialect by out-of-state children, in Labov (ed.), Locating Language in Time and Space, Academic Press, 1980
